_: Cyber Range question bank seed (26 October 2026): 10 per system plus 20 RMF questions for signoff. Written by scripts/author-range-questions.py; edit that script, not this file.

questions.prompt: Which FSMO role makes SBD-DC01 the time source for the whole domain?
questions.explanation: The PDC emulator sits at the top of the domain time hierarchy. SBD-DC02 and every member sync from it; there is no separate time server in this lab.

questions.prompt: How many FSMO roles does a single-domain forest have?
questions.explanation: Schema master, domain naming master, RID master, PDC emulator and infrastructure master. All five can sit on SBD-DC01.

questions.prompt: Where do you check which domain controller holds the PDC emulator role in a console?
options: Active Directory Users and Computers, Operations Masters
questions.explanation: Right-click the domain in Active Directory Users and Computers and open Operations Masters; the PDC tab names the holder.

questions.prompt: Replication between SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 fails with "The target principal name is incorrect." What is the most likely cause?
options: The two controllers are in different sites
A Kerberos problem, such as clock skew or a domain controller machine account password out of sync
questions.explanation: That error is Kerberos failing to authenticate the replication partner. Check time on both controllers first, then the machine account password.

questions.prompt: Which command summarizes replication failures across every domain controller at once?
questions.explanation: repadmin /replsummary lists each controller with its largest delta and failure count. Active Directory Sites and Services shows the same partners in the console.

questions.prompt: SBD-DC02 is restored from a backup older than the tombstone lifetime. What is the right outcome?
options: Treat it as unsafe: demote or forcibly remove it and promote it again
It replicates normally once it boots
Replication catches up faster than usual
questions.explanation: A controller that missed deletions older than the tombstone lifetime can reintroduce lingering objects. It is removed and promoted fresh rather than trusted.

questions.prompt: Where does SBD-DC02 get its time?
questions.explanation: The lab has no separate time server. The second controller and every domain member follow the domain hierarchy up to the PDC emulator.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the time source a domain member is actually using?
questions.explanation: w32tm is the supported tool for the Windows Time service. /query /source names the peer the member follows; /query /status shows the offset.

questions.prompt: How far apart can two clocks be before Kerberos stops working, by default?
questions.explanation: The default maximum tolerance is five minutes. Past that, tickets are rejected and sign-ins fail even though the password is right.

questions.prompt: Which log on a domain controller records a successful domain sign-in?
questions.explanation: Sign-ins, sign-outs and lockouts are Security log events. 4624 is a successful logon; 4625 a failed one; 4740 a lockout.

questions.prompt: Why do the two domain controllers run on different hosts?
options: So one host failing still leaves a domain controller and a DNS server running
questions.explanation: The lab places SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 on separate hosts so the directory and DNS survive a host outage.

questions.prompt: What does SBD-DC02 add that SBD-DC01 alone does not?
options: A second copy of the directory and a second DNS server
questions.explanation: SBD-DC02 is a replica. The PDC emulator, the time source and the CA stay where they are.

questions.prompt: Within one site, how soon does a change on SBD-DC01 reach SBD-DC02 by default?
options: Within seconds, after a change notification
Only when an administrator forces it
questions.explanation: Intra-site replication is notification-based: a controller tells its partners shortly after a change and they pull it.

questions.prompt: What is the default tombstone lifetime for a forest created on current Windows Server versions?
questions.explanation: Forests created on Windows Server 2003 SP1 or later default to 180 days. Older forests may still carry 60.

questions.prompt: Why must a backup used to restore a domain controller be younger than the tombstone lifetime?
options: Kerberos tickets in the backup expire
So deletions made since the backup are still known as tombstones and lingering objects cannot reappear
questions.explanation: Once tombstones are garbage-collected, a restored controller has no record of those deletions and would replicate the objects back.

questions.prompt: Where do the sbd.test DNS zones live in this lab?
options: On both domain controllers, as Active Directory-integrated zones
questions.explanation: DNS runs on the domain controllers. Integrated zones are stored in the directory and replicated with it.

questions.prompt: How do Active Directory-integrated zones reach SBD-DC02?
options: They do not; each controller keeps its own zone
Through directory replication, not a classic zone transfer
questions.explanation: Integrated zones ride along with replication, so every controller running DNS holds a writable copy.

questions.prompt: What does SYSVOL hold that every domain controller must agree on?
options: Group Policy templates and logon scripts
questions.explanation: SYSVOL carries the Group Policy template files and scripts that clients read. If it differs between controllers, policy applies inconsistently.

questions.prompt: Which service replicates SYSVOL between domain controllers on current domains?
questions.explanation: Current domains use DFS Replication for SYSVOL; the older File Replication Service was retired.

questions.prompt: A GPO applies to clients talking to SBD-DC01 but not to those talking to SBD-DC02. Which console check comes first?
options: Group Policy Management, the GPO Status tab, for SYSVOL and directory replication state
questions.explanation: The Status tab compares the GPO on every controller and shows which copy is behind.

questions.prompt: Why does the router need a DHCP relay for workstations on their own VLAN?
options: The router is the DHCP server
A DHCP discover is a broadcast that does not cross VLANs; the relay forwards it to the DHCP server
questions.explanation: Broadcasts stop at the VLAN boundary. The relay, often called an IP helper, turns the discover into a unicast to the server.

questions.prompt: Which UDP ports does DHCP use?
options: 67 on the server and 68 on the client
questions.explanation: DHCP servers listen on UDP 67; clients on UDP 68. The relay must be allowed to reach 67 on the server.

questions.prompt: What does the DHCP "router" option hand a workstation?
options: Its default gateway, the L3 router interface on its VLAN
questions.explanation: Option 3 is the default gateway. The DNS servers come from option 6, and both have to be right for the domain to work.

questions.prompt: A workstation on VLAN 20 pings SBD-DC01, but certificate enrollment against pki.sbd.test on VLAN 30 times out. DNS resolves the name. Which rule fixes it?
options: Permit everything from VLAN 30 to VLAN 20
Add a DHCP relay on VLAN 30
Permit TCP 80 and 443 from VLAN 20 to VLAN 30
Add a static route to VLAN 30
questions.explanation: Enrollment and CRL checks use HTTP and HTTPS to the publication point. The router is the hop that has to allow them.

questions.prompt: Which ports must a domain member reach on a domain controller for Kerberos and LDAP?
questions.explanation: Kerberos uses 88 over both TCP and UDP; LDAP uses TCP 389 (636 for LDAPS). Blocking either breaks sign-in.

questions.prompt: Splunk forwarders stop delivering after a rule change. Which port does forwarder-to-indexer traffic use by default?
questions.explanation: Universal forwarders send to the indexer on TCP 9997 unless changed. 8000 is the web interface and 8089 the management port.

questions.prompt: When a router has several routes to a destination, which one does it use?
options: The one with the highest metric
The most specific match, the longest prefix
questions.explanation: Longest prefix wins. Only when two routes match equally do administrative distance and metric decide.

questions.prompt: What should the default route do in this air-gapped lab?
options: Nothing should leave the enclave; there is no path out
questions.explanation: The network is fully air-gapped. Transfers across the boundary are manual, on approved removable media.

questions.prompt: Which action isolates a compromised VLAN while the rest of the network keeps working?
options: A deny rule for that VLAN on the router’s inter-VLAN interfaces
questions.explanation: The router is the only path between VLANs, so a deny rule there contains the segment without touching the servers.

questions.prompt: If the router blocks a workstation VLAN from reaching the domain controllers, what fails first?
options: Sign-in, because Kerberos and LDAP cannot reach a controller
questions.explanation: Cached credentials may still let a user in, but new sign-ins, Group Policy and DNS all depend on reaching a controller.

questions.prompt: Where is certificate auto-enrollment turned on for domain computers?
options: Group Policy: Computer Configuration, Policies, Windows Settings, Security Settings, Public Key Policies
questions.explanation: The Certificate Services Client, Auto-Enrollment policy under Public Key Policies enables it for every computer the GPO reaches.

questions.prompt: What must a certificate template grant domain computers for auto-enrollment to work?
questions.explanation: All three are checked on the template’s Security tab for the computers’ group. Missing Autoenroll is the most common gap.

questions.prompt: Which console shows the certificates a workstation itself has been issued?
options: certlm.msc, the local computer certificate store
questions.explanation: The local computer store under Personal holds machine certificates. The user store holds the signed-in user’s.

questions.prompt: In a two-tier PKI, why is the root CA kept offline?
options: It is slower than the issuing CA
Its key signs the issuing CA; keeping it offline limits exposure of the trust anchor
questions.explanation: If the root is compromised, every certificate below it is suspect. The issuing CA does the daily work; the root only signs it.

questions.prompt: A workstation reports "the certificate chain could not be built to a trusted root." What is most likely missing?
options: The root or issuing CA certificate in its trust stores, usually published through the directory or Group Policy
questions.explanation: Clients need the root in Trusted Root Certification Authorities and the issuing CA in Intermediate. Publishing to the directory places them automatically.

questions.prompt: Why does certificate validation depend on the clock?
options: Certificates are issued by the time service
Validity periods and the CRL’s next-update time are checked against the current time
questions.explanation: A machine whose clock drifts past a certificate’s validity window, or past the CRL’s next update, fails validation even though nothing was revoked.

questions.prompt: What does a certificate revocation list contain?
options: The serial numbers of revoked certificates, signed by the CA
questions.explanation: Clients download the CRL from the publication point and refuse any certificate whose serial number appears on it.

questions.prompt: Where is the CRL published in this lab?
options: As a web service at pki.sbd.test on VLAN 30, from SBD-PKI-MGMT01
questions.explanation: PKI publication is a VLAN 30 web service on SBD-PKI-MGMT01. The issuing CA and the root stay on their own hosts.

questions.prompt: What does the CDP extension in a certificate point to?
options: Where to download the CRL, such as a URL under pki.sbd.test
questions.explanation: The CRL distribution point tells the client where to fetch revocation data; the AIA extension points to the CA certificate.

questions.prompt: What has to be true for a VLAN 20 workstation to check revocation?
options: Nothing; revocation is checked on the CA
It is signed in as a domain admin
It can resolve pki.sbd.test and reach it over HTTP on VLAN 30
questions.explanation: Revocation checking is a client-side download. Name resolution and the router rule are both in the path.

questions.prompt: Which Windows event shows an account lockout?
questions.explanation: 4740 is logged on the PDC emulator when an account is locked out. 4624 is a successful logon.

questions.prompt: What does an index do in Splunk?
options: Stores events so searches can find them by time and field
questions.explanation: Events land in an index; searches run against it. Retention and access are set per index.

questions.prompt: Which event code finds failed Windows sign-ins?
questions.explanation: 4625 is a failed logon. 4688 is process creation, useful for a different question.

questions.prompt: A domain controller stops appearing in Splunk after a VLAN rule change. Which port must its forwarder reach?
questions.explanation: Receiving is on TCP 9997 by default. 8089 is the management port the deployment server uses; 8000 is the web interface.

questions.prompt: The forwarder runs as a domain account and the Security log stops arriving while other logs continue. What is the gap?
options: The account lacks rights to read the Security log, such as Event Log Readers membership
questions.explanation: The Security log needs explicit read rights. Event Log Readers, or the Manage auditing and security log right, grants them.

questions.prompt: Splunk runs on domain-joined Linux in this lab. What does joining the domain give it?
options: Kerberos sign-in for administrators and a trusted hostname in DNS
questions.explanation: Domain-joined Linux lets administrators use their directory accounts and gives the host a registered name the forwarders can trust.

questions.prompt: What decides how long events stay searchable?
options: The index’s retention settings: maximum size and maximum age
questions.explanation: Each index has a size cap and an age limit. When either is hit, the oldest bucket is frozen, deleted or archived.

questions.prompt: Events are to stay searchable for 90 days, then be archived. Where is that configured?
options: In the index’s settings on the indexer
questions.explanation: Retention is an index property on the indexer; forwarders only ship events.

questions.prompt: Ten failed sign-ins against one account within five minutes should raise an alert. Which Splunk feature does that?
options: A scheduled saved search with an alert condition
questions.explanation: Alerts are saved searches on a schedule with a trigger condition, such as a count over a threshold per account.

questions.prompt: Why forward the domain controllers’ Security log, not just the System log?
options: Sign-ins, lockouts and privilege use are recorded in the Security log
questions.explanation: The System log covers services and drivers. Account activity, the thing a security team watches, is in the Security log.

questions.prompt: What does a discovery scan find?
options: Live hosts and their open ports
questions.explanation: Discovery maps what is on the network before a vulnerability scan looks deeper at each host.

questions.prompt: Why does the scanner run inside the enclave rather than from outside?
options: The network is air-gapped; there is no path in from outside
questions.explanation: Nothing crosses the air gap automatically, so the scanner lives on the network it assesses.

questions.prompt: What does the CVSS score on a finding express?
options: How severe the vulnerability is, from 0 to 10
questions.explanation: CVSS rates severity. The plugin output says what was found; the score helps decide what to fix first.

questions.prompt: Why does a credentialed scan find more than an unauthenticated one?
options: It signs in and checks installed software, patches and settings directly
questions.explanation: Without credentials the scanner can only infer from the outside. With them it reads the host’s own state.

questions.prompt: Which account design fits a Windows credentialed scan in a tiered administration model?
options: A dedicated scan account with local administrator rights on the hosts it scans, never a Domain Admin
questions.explanation: A scanning account touches every host, so it is kept out of the top tier and limited to what the scan needs.

questions.prompt: A credentialed scan of the domain controllers reports a sign-in failure although the password is right. Which lab fact matters first?
options: The CA has not issued it a certificate
Time: if the scanner’s clock drifts from the domain, Kerberos rejects it
questions.explanation: Nessus is domain-joined Linux here, so it follows the domain time hierarchy. More than five minutes of skew and Kerberos refuses the login.

questions.prompt: How do plugin updates reach an air-gapped scanner?
options: Downloaded outside, moved in on approved removable media, and applied offline
questions.explanation: Every transfer across the boundary is manual and human-controlled. Plugins, content and patches all come in the same way.

questions.prompt: Why does plugin age matter?
options: New vulnerabilities are not detected until the plugins that check for them arrive
questions.explanation: A scan is only as current as its plugins. The date of the last update is part of the evidence.

questions.prompt: How is a confirmed false positive handled?
options: Documented and marked so later reports exclude it, with the evidence kept
questions.explanation: A finding can be wrong, but the decision to dismiss it is itself evidence. It stays on record with the reason.

questions.prompt: What does a compliance scan against a STIG give you?
options: A pass or fail per check against the host’s configuration
questions.explanation: Compliance audits compare settings to the benchmark. Vulnerability plugins and compliance checks are different scan types.

questions.prompt: What does the management agent on an endpoint do?
options: Talks to ePO to pull policies and report status
questions.explanation: The agent is the endpoint’s side of the conversation. No agent, no policy and no reporting.

questions.prompt: How can the agent reach every domain-joined workstation at once?
options: Hand it out through a DHCP option
Carry it on a USB drive to each machine
Deploy it through Group Policy or an ePO push using domain credentials
questions.explanation: Both routes lean on the directory: Group Policy software installation, or a push that signs in with a domain account.

questions.prompt: Why is there one ePO instance in this lab?
options: One enclave, one console: its policies and repository cover every endpoint
One per VLAN is not allowed
questions.explanation: The lab keeps Splunk, Nessus and ePO as single instances. The System Hub shows where each one sits.

questions.prompt: An endpoint still shows the old policy after a change. Which agent action comes first?
options: Remove it from the system tree
An agent wake-up: collect and send properties, then enforce policies
questions.explanation: The agent polls on its interval. A wake-up forces the conversation now, and the policy enforcement follows.

questions.prompt: Why synchronize the ePO system tree with Active Directory?
options: So endpoints are grouped by organizational unit and policies follow the directory structure
questions.explanation: A tree that mirrors the OUs lets one policy assignment cover the right machines, the same way a GPO link does.

questions.prompt: A policy assigned to a parent group never reaches a child group. Why?
options: The agent is out of date
Inheritance was broken on the child group
questions.explanation: Policies inherit down the tree unless a group breaks inheritance. Check the child group’s assigned policies for the override.

questions.prompt: How does an air-gapped ePO get content and engine updates?
options: Pulled outside, moved in on approved removable media, and checked into the master repository
questions.explanation: Same rule as plugins and patches: a human carries it across the boundary, then it is checked in.

questions.prompt: What does a distributed repository do?
options: Serves content to endpoints nearer to them and takes load off the ePO server
questions.explanation: Repositories hold content; the master is the source of truth and distributed copies serve it out.

questions.prompt: What does a quarantine or isolation policy do to a suspect endpoint?
options: Blocks its traffic except to ePO so it can be investigated
questions.explanation: The host stays reachable by the management server and nothing else, which keeps the evidence and stops the spread.

questions.prompt: Which evidence shows the agent on a host is current?
options: Its last communication time and version in the system tree
questions.explanation: The system tree lists each managed host with the agent version and the last time it checked in.

questions.prompt: Which publication defines the Risk Management Framework steps?
questions.explanation: SP 800-37 Rev. 2 is the RMF itself. SP 800-53 supplies the controls it selects from.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: Which publication supplies the control catalog this lab uses?
questions.explanation: SP 800-53 Rev. 5 is the catalog; SP 800-53B holds the federal baselines.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: Which step did SP 800-37 Revision 2 add?
questions.explanation: Prepare was added at the organization and system level. The public 2016 JSIG predates it and describes six steps.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: What follows Categorize in the RMF?
questions.explanation: Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor, with Prepare ahead of them in Rev. 2.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: This lab’s system is categorized Moderate, Low, Low. What does that mean?
options: Moderate confidentiality, low integrity, low availability
questions.explanation: The three values are the CIA impact levels. The owner’s categorization is planning input, not a completed assessment.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: Who makes the authorization decision?
questions.explanation: The AO accepts the risk and signs the decision. Everyone else prepares, implements, assesses or recommends.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: What is a POA&M?
options: A plan of action and milestones for weaknesses that are not yet corrected
questions.explanation: Each open weakness gets a planned fix, resources, milestones and a date, and the AO sees it with the package.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: What does the system security plan document?
options: How the system implements its selected controls
questions.explanation: The SSP describes the system, its boundary and each control’s implementation. It is the heart of the package.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: What does the assessor produce?
questions.explanation: The SAR records what was tested, how, and what was found. Its findings feed the POA&M.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: How is the JSIG framed in this lab?
options: SAP-specific implementation direction for the NIST RMF, used with CNSSI 1253
questions.explanation: NIST is the foundation; the JSIG says how special access programs apply it, together with CNSSI 1253 and AO direction.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: Which instruction provides categorization and control selection for national security systems?
questions.explanation: CNSSI 1253 supplies the national security system overlays and selection; it is not a Moderate baseline from SP 800-53B.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: What is continuous monitoring for?
options: Keeping the authorization current by tracking control effectiveness and changes
questions.explanation: Monitor is the step that never ends: ongoing assessments, change tracking and reporting keep the risk picture current.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: Which control family is AC?
questions.explanation: AC is Access Control. AU is Audit and Accountability; AT is Awareness and Training; CA is Assessment, Authorization and Monitoring.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: Which control family is AU?
questions.explanation: AU covers audit records, logging and review, the family Splunk evidence maps to.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: Which control family is CM?
questions.explanation: CM is Configuration Management: baselines, change control and the settings STIGs enforce. CP is Contingency Planning.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: What is an authorization with conditions?
options: An authorization granted while specified weaknesses are tracked to completion
questions.explanation: The AO accepts the risk for now and the conditions, usually POA&M items with dates, stay on the record.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: What is the Body of Evidence?
options: The collected artifacts that show controls are implemented and working
questions.explanation: Policies, procedures, configurations, scan results, screenshots and logs: whatever proves a control, kept and maintained.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: Which role owns the system’s day-to-day security posture?
questions.explanation: The Information System Security Officer runs the system’s security operations; the ISSM manages the program; the SCA assesses.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: What triggers a review of an existing authorization?
options: A significant change to the system or its environment
questions.explanation: Significant changes, such as a new boundary, new interconnections or a changed categorization, send the system back through the relevant steps.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG

questions.prompt: How do evidence artifacts leave this air-gapped enclave?
options: By manual, human-controlled transfer on approved removable media
questions.explanation: The lab’s baseline: no physical connection or automated path crosses the air gap.
questions.source: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, SP 800-53 Rev. 5, the 2016 JSIG
